title: Study and Teaching
hookLine: one question: does a holy text open on your own?
carry: svadhyaya: holy study goes with a guide
tomorrow: Priya copies half of Nani's line. which of the week's marks are in it?

cards: So much can be learned alone now: a video for fixing a sink, an app for chords, a course at two in the morning. Learning the letters can go that way too.
But the letters are a door into texts people have lived by for a long time. So here's the question: once you can read a holy text, can you read it on your own?

teach.b: The Taittiriya Upanishad answers with a rhythm. One passage lists what a good life holds: right conduct, truth, discipline, calm, welcoming guests. And after every single one, the same refrain: and study and teaching.

Svadhyaya and pravachana. Reading for yourself, and receiving it from someone and handing it on, always together. When students finish, the teacher's parting words include: don't neglect study and teaching.

teach.h: ASK, SERVE, LEARN FROM ONE WHO HAS SEEN.
teach.b: And in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to learn by bowing, by asking, by serving; those who have seen the truth will teach you.

That teacher is the guru, and it's why many Hindus keep a day, Guru Purnima, to thank the ones who taught them. So the tradition's answer: read it yourself, yes, and also with someone who has lived inside it.

A neighbor says something close. In the book of Acts, a traveler from Ethiopia is riding home, reading the prophet Isaiah aloud in his chariot. Philip runs alongside and asks: "Understandest thou what thou readest?"

teach.h: ACTS: HOW CAN I, EXCEPT SOME MAN GUIDE ME?
teach.b: The traveler answers: "How can I, except some man should guide me?" And he invites Philip up to sit beside him.
Shared: two traditions that say a holy text opens best with a guide. And an honest difference. In Acts, Philip reads Isaiah as pointing to Jesus, and the story ends with the traveler baptized.
In the Gita, the guide is a teacher who has seen the truth, and the learning goes on through asking and serving.

how: Many Hindus first learn a text like the Gita with a teacher or an elder, verse by verse, often in a class or a study group, alongside reading it on their own.

games.q: a friend has been reading the Gita alone for a month and feels stuck in chapter two. what fits both the Taittiriya and the Gita?
o: keep reading, and find someone who has lived inside it to read with.

push on alone; asking for help means you didn't try.
games.why: study and teaching go together, the Taittiriya says, and the Gita sends Arjuna to ask those who have seen. a guide doesn't replace reading; it opens it.

practice: Let your eyes close and bring to mind one person who once explained something so it finally made sense. See their face, their hands, the place you were sitting.
Stay there with them quietly; if you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own words.
